screens.title: Physics Materials and Forces
screens.subtitle: Tune surface behavior and apply forces precisely for predictable, tactile interactions

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson we explore two tightly linked parts of Unity physics: Physics Materials, which define how surfaces interact at contact, and the different ways you can apply forces and torque to rigid bodies. You will learn what dynamic and static friction mean, how bounciness conserves collision energy, and how combine modes decide the final friction or bounce when two materials meet. We will also walk through the practical differences between applying continuous force, instant impulses, mass‑independent velocity changes, and mass‑independent acceleration. You will see concrete examples: a bouncy ball using a high restitution material, a slippery plane using low friction, and a rocket that uses continuous thrust and torque. Along the way I will point out common mistakes like applying physics in the wrong update loop or forgetting to choose an appropriate ForceMode. By the end, you will know how to create materials, assign them to colliders, pick a ForceMode for a desired feel, and implement a reliable input pattern with FixedUpdate so physics behaves the same on every machine. Think about one gameplay feel you want to tune — is it slippery, sticky, or springy? We'll build toward that.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Physics Materials and ForceMode selection let you control tactile gameplay: from slippery ice to bouncy trampolines and consistent thrust-driven motion.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to create and tune Physics Materials so surfaces behave as intended, and apply them to colliders to control sliding and bouncing. You will also apply forces correctly: use Rigidbody. AddForce for continuous thrust, AddTorque for rotation, and choose between Force, Impulse, VelocityChange, and Acceleration according to whether you need mass-dependent or mass-independent effects. An important practical skill is separating input detection from physics application — detect input in Update but apply forces in FixedUpdate, or use a request flag pattern so jumps and impulses are reliable. Finally, you will learn to identify common mistakes such as applying forces in Update, omitting ForceMode and relying on the default behavior, or starting objects with overlapping colliders that cause physics explosions. Each objective maps to a verified milestone where you will demonstrate a bouncy ball, a slippery surface, and a rocket that responds consistently to thrust and spin. These skills are essential because they turn abstract physics parameters into tangible game feel that players perceive every frame.

screens.title: What is a Physics Material?
screens.subtitle: An asset that controls friction and bounciness at contacts

narration.text: A Physics Material in Unity is a project asset that encodes how two surfaces interact when they collide. Conceptually, it describes three main measurable properties: dynamic friction, static friction, and bounciness. Dynamic friction determines the resistance while surfaces slide past each other; if it's set to zero the surface behaves like ice. Static friction resists the start of motion and prevents objects from sliding down gentle slopes until a threshold is reached — in many cases static friction is slightly higher than dynamic friction. Bounciness, also called restitution, controls how much kinetic energy is conserved during a collision: zero means no bounce, and one means a perfectly elastic collision. Each material also exposes combine modes for friction and bounce. Combine modes decide how the engine blends two materials during contact — average, minimum, maximum, or multiply — and this controls surprising outcomes when different materials meet. For example, a highly bouncy ball colliding with a nonbouncy floor may behave differently depending on using Maximum versus Minimum as the bounce combine. A common misconception is to think bounciness alone determines bounce height; in reality mass, velocity, and the chosen combine mode all influence the result. Key takeaway: Physics Materials give you deterministic knobs to shape how collisions feel and conserve energy.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Physics Material defines friction and bounciness and how those values combine between colliding surfaces.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is a Physics Material?
Definition & properties
Physics Materials expose Dynamic Friction, Static Friction, and Bounciness. They also provide Friction Combine and Bounce Combine choices which determine how two materials blend during collision. These settings let you model surfaces from ice to rubber to springs.
Dynamic Friction
Resistance while sliding. 0 means no sliding resistance, 1 means strong resistance.
Static Friction
Resistance preventing initial motion. Often slightly higher than dynamic friction.
Bounciness
Amount of energy conserved in a collision. 0 is dead, 1 is perfectly elastic.
Combine Modes explained
  • Average: mean of the two values.
  • Minimum: uses the smaller value, good for slippery interactions.
  • Maximum: uses the larger value, preserves stickiness or bounce.
  • Multiply: multiplies values for compounded effects.
Concrete example
Create a 'BouncyMaterial' with bounciness 0.9 and Bounce Combine set to Maximum. Assign it to a sphere's collider and drop it onto a plane. Observe the high bounce retained by Maximum combine.
Key Takeaway

Physics Materials are the first control over contact behavior. Combine modes resolve interactions when two materials meet.

screens.title: Create and Apply a Physics Material
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step workflow from asset to collider assignment

narration.text: Creating and applying a Physics Material follows a consistent workflow. First, create the material asset in the Project window by choosing Create then Physics Material. Next, configure the asset's properties: set Dynamic Friction, Static Friction, and Bounciness to values that reflect the surface you want. Choose Friction Combine and Bounce Combine depending on how this material should interact with others. Third, select the GameObject that has a Collider component and assign the material to its Material slot in the Collider inspector. If both colliders have materials, their combine modes determine the resulting contact response. Finally, enter Play mode and observe contacts; tweak the material and re-test until the behavior matches your intended feel. A concrete example: create a 'SlipperyMaterial' with Dynamic and Static Friction at 0.1 and Friction Combine set to Minimum, assign it to a plane, then drop a sphere with a normal material onto it to verify sliding. A common mistake is to adjust the material but forget to assign it to the collider or to test with objects that are initially overlapping — always check initial placements. This stepwise pattern ensures predictable, testable surface behavior.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Create → configure → assign → test → iterate. Ensure no overlapping colliders and verify combine mode outcomes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Create and Apply a Physics Material
Step-by-step
1. Create: Project → Create → Physics Material.
2. Configure: set dynamic/static friction and bounciness; pick combine modes.
3. Assign: drag the material into the Collider's Material slot.
4. Test: Play and observe; iterate values for desired feel.
Common mistake
Changing a material asset does not affect colliders if the asset isn't assigned. Also avoid starting objects with overlapping colliders.
Concrete scenario
Create 'SlipperyMaterial' with both frictions at 0.1 and Friction Combine set to Minimum. Assign it to the plane. Drop a sphere and observe extended sliding and reduced deceleration.
Key Takeaway

Follow the create-configure-assign-test loop. Combine modes are critical when mixed materials meet.

screens.title: Friction: Dynamic vs Static
screens.subtitle: How friction values affect sliding and initiation of motion

narration.text: Friction appears in two flavors in Unity Physics Materials: dynamic and static. Dynamic friction is the coefficient applied while two surfaces move relative to each other. It reduces sliding velocity over time, and on slippery surfaces it is close to zero. Static friction is the coefficient that resists the start of sliding when surfaces are at rest relative to each other. Think of static friction as the force that keeps a box from starting to slide on a slightly tilted ramp. It is typically equal to or higher than dynamic friction. In gameplay, setting static friction too high can make objects stick unexpectedly, while setting dynamic friction too high can make motion feel sluggish. Another important point is how combine modes interact: using Minimum for friction between a slippery plane and a rubber object will favor slippery behavior, while Maximum would preserve a sticky interaction. A common misconception is to adjust only dynamic friction when an object won't start sliding; if an object never overcomes static friction, increase velocity or reduce static friction rather than only tuning dynamic friction. Try a test by creating two materials with differing friction and watch how combine modes change behavior.

keyIdea.title: Friction rule
keyIdea.text: Static friction prevents start of motion; dynamic friction governs motion while sliding. Combine modes resolve mixed-material interactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Friction: Dynamic vs Static
Concept & impact
Static friction resists starting motion; dynamic friction slows sliding. These two coefficients control how objects begin moving and how they slow down once in motion. Adjust both to tune whether a surface feels sticky, normal, or slippery.
Tip
If an object won’t start sliding, reduce static friction or increase the applied force instead of only modifying dynamic friction.
Example scenario
A crate on a ramp stays put. Increasing dynamic friction will not help; static friction is preventing motion. Lower static friction or increase incline to see sliding begin.
Check your understanding
  • Why might a heavy object still slide on low-friction surfaces?
  • How do combine modes affect a rubber ball hitting ice?
Key Takeaway

Tune static friction to control motion start and dynamic friction to control sliding feel. Combine modes decide the final result when two materials meet.

screens.title: Bounciness and Bounce Combine
screens.subtitle: How restitution conserves energy and how combine modes shape bounce

narration.text: Bounciness, also called restitution, controls how much kinetic energy a collision conserves. A value of zero absorbs all impact energy so the object does not bounce, while a value near one tries to conserve most energy and produces high rebounds. However, the actual bounce you observe depends on both colliding materials and their Bounce Combine setting. Combine modes are Average, Minimum, Maximum, and Multiply. Average takes the mean of two bounciness values, Minimum favors the less bouncy surface, Maximum preserves high bounce when one material is very springy, and Multiply scales values multiplicatively. For a 'BouncyMaterial' with 0.9 bounciness colliding with a sticky floor of 0.1, a Maximum combine will yield a higher bounce than Minimum. A common misconception is to expect perfect energy conservation when setting bounciness to one; in practice, mass distribution and contact resolution influence height, and collision damping or constraints may limit rebound. When tuning trampoline or vehicle suspension effects, combine mode and object mass interact to produce the final result, so iterative testing in Play mode is essential. Bounciness and Bounce Combine means high bounciness aims to conserve energy, but combine modes and mass determine the actual rebound behavior.. In practical terms, how restitution conserves energy and how combine modes shape bounce. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bounce insight
keyIdea.text: High bounciness aims to conserve energy, but combine modes and mass determine the actual rebound behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Bounciness and Bounce Combine
Bounciness explained
Bounciness sets restitution at collisions. Use high values for trampoline-like behavior and low values for damped impacts. Combine this with Bounce Combine to define how two materials share bounce influence.
Use Case
Trampolines, bouncy pickups, and rubber balls.
Caution
Expect differences due to mass and collision solver damping; bounciness alone does not guarantee identical bounce height across objects.
Concrete example
Set 'BouncyMaterial' bounciness to 0.9 and Bounce Combine to Maximum. Assign to a sphere and drop on a low‑bounce plane to see the sphere retain high rebound.
Key Takeaway

Bounciness controls restitution but combine modes and object properties determine the observed rebound; test and iterate.

screens.title: Force Application Methods
screens.subtitle: Rigidbody.AddForce, AddTorque and where to call them

narration.text: Applying forces in Unity is centered on Rigidbody methods: AddForce for linear forces and AddTorque for rotational forces. These operations alter a Rigidbody's velocity or angular velocity depending on the chosen ForceMode. The most important engine-level detail is to perform physics modifications in FixedUpdate. FixedUpdate runs at fixed time steps that the physics engine uses for deterministic simulation. If you apply forces in Update, which runs once per rendered frame and varies with frame rate, you will produce inconsistent behavior across machines. A robust pattern is to detect input in Update and set simple boolean flags or desired vectors, then consume those flags in FixedUpdate and call AddForce or AddTorque there. For example, set a jumpRequested flag in Update when Space is pressed, then in FixedUpdate add an Impulse to the Rigidbody and reset the flag. For continuous thrust, check GetKey in Update or use a continuous flag consumed in FixedUpdate, and call AddForce with ForceMode. Force inside FixedUpdate. Common misconception: using GetKeyDown inside FixedUpdate will sometimes miss input; use Update to capture instant input events and then apply forces in FixedUpdate. Reliable separation yields consistent feel and reproducible debugging.

keyIdea.title: Where to apply forces
keyIdea.text: Detect input in Update, apply forces in FixedUpdate using AddForce/AddTorque; this ensures consistent physics timing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Force Application Methods
Core methods
  • AddForce: linear force to move a Rigidbody.
  • AddTorque: rotational force to spin a Rigidbody.
Best practice: detect input in Update, set flags, then apply forces in FixedUpdate. This pattern prevents frame-rate-dependent physics differences.
Concrete code pattern (conceptual)
// Update: capture input
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) jumpRequested = true;

// FixedUpdate: apply physics
if (jumpRequested) { rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpImpulse, ForceMode.Impulse); jumpRequested = false; }
Common Mistake

Applying forces in Update can make physics inconsistent across frame rates. Use FixedUpdate for physics calls and Update for input detection.

screens.title: ForceMode.Force and Continuous Forces
screens.subtitle: Continuous, mass-dependent forces such as thrust or wind

narration.text: ForceMode. Force applies a continuous force that is scaled by the Rigidbody's mass. Use it when you want acceleration that respects mass differences, like a rocket engine or persistent wind. Because the effect is accumulated over time, calling AddForce with ForceMode. Force every FixedUpdate while a control is held results in gradual acceleration. An example is holding the 'W' key to apply thrust along the transform's forward direction. The practical effect: heavier objects accelerate more slowly under ForceMode. Force when given the same force vector, which matches real-world intuition. A common pitfall is using large per-frame forces instead of reasonable magnitudes; this can push objects too quickly or destabilize the physics solver. Also remember to apply forces in FixedUpdate. If you need a mass‑independent continuous acceleration, use ForceMode. Acceleration instead. To test, create a rocket cube with a Rigidbody, call AddForce(transform. forward * thrust, ForceMode. Force) while the key is held, and observe how acceleration ramps up. Ask yourself: do you want object mass to affect acceleration in this gameplay moment? If yes, ForceMode. Force is the right choice. ForceMode.Force and Continuous Forces means forcemode.force results in mass-dependent acceleration; apply it in fixedupdate for thrust-like effects.. In practical terms, continuous, mass-dependent forces such as thrust or wind. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Continuous force
keyIdea.text: ForceMode.Force results in mass-dependent acceleration; apply it in FixedUpdate for thrust-like effects.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ForceMode.Force and Continuous Forces
Behavior
ForceMode.Force applies a force each physics step and is scaled by mass. It's ideal for sustained acceleration like engines or wind pushes. Over multiple FixedUpdates, velocity increases gradually.
Tip: tune thrust magnitudes conservatively and observe solver stability. Use damping if motion feels too floaty.
Concrete example
// In FixedUpdate
if (thrusting) rb.AddForce(transform.forward * rocketThrust, ForceMode.Force);
Hold the thrust key and watch the cube steadily pick up speed. Heavier mass -> slower acceleration under the same rocketThrust value.
Key Takeaway

Use ForceMode.Force for continuous, mass-sensitive acceleration. Keep input capture separate from physics application.

screens.title: ForceMode.Impulse and Instant Forces
screens.subtitle: Immediate, mass-dependent velocity changes for jumps and impacts

narration.text: ForceMode. Impulse applies an immediate change in momentum and respects the Rigidbody's mass. This is perfect for one‑time bursts like jump impulses, explosions, or collision knockbacks. Because the change uses mass, a heavier character will receive a smaller velocity change for the same impulse vector than a lighter one. The usual pattern is to detect the instant input in Update (for example GetKeyDown) and set a flag, then in FixedUpdate apply AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse once to perform the action, and clear the flag. The ForceApplier example shows this: when a jump is requested, AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpImpulse, ForceMode. Impulse) yields an instant upward velocity change. A common mistake is to rely on default ForceMode. Force for instant events, which produces gradual acceleration instead of a crisp jump. Another pitfall is detecting GetKeyDown inside FixedUpdate — it can miss the input. Always capture the event in Update or use an event queue then apply the impulse in FixedUpdate. After applying an impulse, observe the behavior and adjust the impulse magnitude to account for player mass and desired airtime. ForceMode.Impulse and Instant Forces means forcemode.impulse performs an immediate, mass-dependent momentum change — ideal for jumps and explosions.. In practical terms, immediate, mass-dependent velocity changes for jumps and impacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instant mass-based change
keyIdea.text: ForceMode.Impulse performs an immediate, mass-dependent momentum change — ideal for jumps and explosions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ForceMode.Impulse and Instant Forces
Behavior
Impulse changes momentum instantly and depends on mass. Use it for discrete events like jumps or sudden pushes from explosions.
Pattern: detect button press in Update, set a request flag, then apply AddForce with ForceMode.Impulse in FixedUpdate and clear the flag.
Example snippet
// Update
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) jumpRequested = true;

// FixedUpdate
if (jumpRequested) { rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpImpulse, ForceMode.Impulse); jumpRequested = false; }
Misconception

Using default ForceMode for an instant action will not produce the immediate velocity change you expect. Choose Impulse for crisp responses.

screens.title: VelocityChange vs Acceleration
screens.subtitle: Mass-independent options and when to use them

narration.text: VelocityChange and Acceleration are the mass‑independent ForceMode options you use when you want the same effect regardless of object mass. ForceMode. VelocityChange applies an immediate change in velocity ignoring mass. Use it when you want an instant, identical speed set for light and heavy objects — for example a mid‑air boost that should feel the same whether the character is carrying a heavy item or not. ForceMode. Acceleration applies a continuous acceleration that ignores the object's mass, so a light and heavy body accelerate identically under the same input. Acceleration can be useful for artificial gravity effects or mass-agnostic environmental accelerations. The trade-offs: VelocityChange is abrupt and can feel less physically realistic; Acceleration removes natural mass-based differentiation. A common error is to confuse VelocityChange with Impulse — remember that Impulse respects mass, while VelocityChange does not. When designing gameplay, ask whether mass should change the outcome. If it should, prefer Force or Impulse. If it should not, prefer VelocityChange or Acceleration. Test both in small scenes to see the feel and choose the option that best matches gameplay intention. VelocityChange vs Acceleration means use velocitychange for instant mass-independent velocity edits and acceleration for continuous mass‑independent acceleration.. In practical terms, mass-independent options and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mass-independent forces
keyIdea.text: Use VelocityChange for instant mass-independent velocity edits and Acceleration for continuous mass‑independent acceleration.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › VelocityChange vs Acceleration
ForceMode.VelocityChange
Applies an immediate change to velocity and ignores mass. Use for instant, identical boosts across different masses.
Example: a mid-air dash that must feel identical whether the player is light or heavy.
ForceMode.Acceleration
Applies continuous acceleration ignoring mass. Use for consistent acceleration effects like controlled levitation or engineless drift.
Example: environmental acceleration that should move all objects equally regardless of mass.
Comparison Summary

VelocityChange is an instant, mass-ignoring velocity edit. Acceleration is a continuous, mass-ignoring acceleration. Choose based on whether you need an instant set or ongoing acceleration and whether mass should matter.

screens.title: ForceApplier Example Pattern
screens.subtitle: Reliable input detection and physics application for thrust, jump, and spin

narration.text: Let's review the ForceApplier script pattern you will implement. The script first gets the Rigidbody in Start and disables itself if no Rigidbody exists. For input, it uses Update to capture instant events such as a jump key press and sets a boolean request flag. FixedUpdate is used for all physics operations: continuous thrust with AddForce(transform. forward * rocketThrust, ForceMode. Force) while a key is held, an instant jump using AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpImpulse, ForceMode. Impulse) when the jumpRequested flag is set, and continuous torque using AddTorque for spin. The important lesson is separation: input detection in Update and physics application in FixedUpdate. The script also demonstrates a common mistake in comments — checking GetKeyDown in FixedUpdate — and shows the correct flag approach. When tuning values, adjust jumpImpulse and rocketThrust in the Inspector and observe effect across different rigidbody masses. This pattern prevents missed inputs on high frame rates and inconsistent forces on low frame rates. Try implementing the script, attach it to the Rocket cube, and iteratively tune parameters while watching debug logs indicating when each force is applied.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Update to capture input flags and FixedUpdate to apply AddForce/AddTorque calls. Tune magnitudes in the Inspector.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ForceApplier Example Pattern
Conceptual code view
public class ForceApplier : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float jumpImpulse = 10f;
    public float rocketThrust = 5f;
    public float spinTorque = 2f;

    private Rigidbody rb;
    private bool jumpRequested = false;

    void Start() { rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>(); }

    void Update() { if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) jumpRequested = true; }

    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W)) rb.AddForce(transform.forward * rocketThrust, ForceMode.Force);
        if (jumpRequested) { rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpImpulse, ForceMode.Impulse); jumpRequested = false; }
        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.E)) rb.AddTorque(Vector3.up * spinTorque, ForceMode.Force);
    }
}
Adjust parameters in the Inspector and watch debug logs when forces are applied to confirm behavior.
Concrete scenario
Attach this script to the Rocket cube. Hold 'W' for thrust, press 'Space' for an impulse jump, and hold 'E' to spin. Observe different motion patterns and tune magnitudes.
Pro Tip

Use small debug logs to indicate when each force is applied so you can verify the Update-to-FixedUpdate interaction.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
screens.subtitle: Avoiding frame-rate issues, incorrect ForceMode use, and collider overlap

narration.text: When working with Physics Materials and forces, a few common mistakes repeatedly slow development and create inconsistent gameplay. First, applying forces in Update instead of FixedUpdate leads to frame-rate-dependent physics. The fix is to detect input in Update and set flags consumed by FixedUpdate. Second, omitting a ForceMode or assuming the default will behave like an impulse can produce gradual acceleration instead of an instant velocity change; be deliberate when choosing between Force, Impulse, VelocityChange, and Acceleration. Third, overlapping colliders at scene start cause the solver to apply corrective forces that look like explosions; avoid initial overlaps and use discrete steps to place objects. Fourth, forgetting that combine modes can dramatically change surface behavior — mixing a high-bounce object with a low-bounce surface will not always produce the high bounce you expect if the combine mode favors the minimum. For debugging: add concise debug logs when forces are applied, view Rigidbody mass and velocities in the Inspector during Play, and simplify tests to single interactions. These practices make physics behavior transparent and reproducible across machines. Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips means use update for input, fixedupdate for physics, pick forcemode intentionally, and check for overlapping colliders at scene start.. In practical terms, avoiding frame-rate issues, incorrect forcemode use, and collider overlap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debugging rules
keyIdea.text: Use Update for input, FixedUpdate for physics, pick ForceMode intentionally, and check for overlapping colliders at scene start.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
Frequent issues
  • Applying forces in Update causes inconsistent physics.
  • Using default ForceMode for instant effects leads to wrong behavior.
  • Overlapping colliders at startup cause extreme solver corrections.
  • Not testing combine modes when mixing materials.
Debug Tip
Log when forces fire and inspect velocity in Play mode.
Test Tip
Simplify to a single sphere-plane interaction to validate material settings.
Placement Tip
Ensure initial positions don't overlap to avoid corrective impulses on start.
Key Takeaway

Clear separation of input and physics, intentional ForceMode selection, and careful initial placement reduce unpredictable physics and make tuning faster.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to carry forward

narration.text: Let's summarize three core ideas you should remember. First, Physics Materials define dynamic friction, static friction, and bounciness, and combine modes determine how two materials interact during collisions. Second, choose ForceMode deliberately: Force and Impulse are mass-dependent for continuous thrust and instant momentum changes respectively; VelocityChange and Acceleration ignore mass when you need identical effects across objects. Third, always separate input detection from physics application — capture events in Update, set a request flag, and apply forces in FixedUpdate to ensure consistent, frame-rate-independent behavior. These three concepts—material tuning, force mode selection, and the Update-to-FixedUpdate pattern—are the practical toolkit you will use to shape the tactile feel of movement and collisions in your projects. When you need a quick check, ask: does mass matter for this effect? Should this be instant or continuous? Will this action be triggered by one input event or held input?
